q: Zinfandel's DNA trail ends at which Croatian variety, and what is that grape's historical name?
accept: crljenak kastelanski also known as tribidrag
tribidrag or crljenak kastelanski from croatia
crljenak kastelanski the same grape as primitivo
tribidrag from dalmatia identical to primitivo
a croatian grape called crljenak kastelanski whose old name is tribidrag
ans: Crljenak Kaštelanski, later shown to be the ancient Dalmatian variety Tribidrag (Kratošija in Montenegro) — the same grape as Italy's Primitivo
exp: Carole Meredith's UC Davis lab matched Zinfandel to Primitivo in 1994, then in December 2001 found a handful of surviving vines called Crljenak Kaštelanski in a garden at Kaštela on the Dalmatian coast; further work tied that to Tribidrag, documented in Croatian records from the early sixteenth century. The takeaway for a candidate is that Zinfandel is an old Adriatic variety with an American career, not an American variety — which is why Primitivo tastes like a cousin rather than a copy.

q: A California wine labeled with both a vintage and an AVA must legally contain at least:
opts: 75% of the stated vintage and 85% from the named AVA
95% of the stated vintage and 85% from the named AVA
85% of the stated vintage and 95% from the named AVA
100% of the stated vintage and 100% from the named AVA
exp: Federal law sets 85% for an AVA and, when an AVA is named, 95% for the vintage; a broader state or country appellation needs only 85% of the stated vintage. The varietal minimum is a separate figure again — 75% federally, which is why so many 'Cabernet Sauvignon' bottlings carry undeclared Merlot or Petit Verdot. California then goes beyond the federal floor: state law requires 100% California fruit for a wine labeled with the California appellation, stricter than the 75% the TTB would allow.

q: Which Mendocino AVA's fog-bound 'deep end' persuaded Louis Roederer to found a California sparkling estate in 1982?
ans: Anderson Valley — Roederer Estate at Philo
exp: The valley runs northwest toward the sea at Navarro and marine air pushes up it, so the coolest ground is the 'deep end' at the Navarro end, while Boonville and Yorkville to the southeast are warmer. The name is the trap: 'deep end' sounds like the far interior and in fact means the seaward, foggiest stretch. Roederer chose it for the long hang time and naturally high acid a base wine needs, and unusually for a Champagne outpost it planted its own vineyards rather than buying fruit. The same cold suits Alsatian whites: Navarro Vineyards' Gewurztraminer and Riesling are the other Anderson Valley signature.

q: Which rootstock's collapse forced the replanting of most of Napa and Sonoma from the late 1980s, and why did it fail?
accept: axr1 failed because of its vinifera parentage and phylloxera biotype b
ax r number one was only partly resistant and biotype b broke it
axr#1 had aramon in its parentage so phylloxera overcame it
axr1 the uc davis recommendation that fell to biotype b phylloxera
ans: AXR#1 (Aramon × Rupestris Ganzin No. 1). Its vinifera parent left it only partially resistant, and a phylloxera strain known as biotype B overcame it; growers replanted to fully resistant stocks such as St. George, 110R, 1103P, 101-14, 3309C and 5C
exp: UC Davis had recommended AXR#1 for vigour and yield, ignoring the rule French growers had learned a century earlier: never build a rootstock on a vinifera parent. Roughly two thirds of Napa was pulled and replanted through the 1990s at a cost in the billions — and the disaster doubled as an upgrade, since the replant brought better clones, tighter spacing and vertical trellising in one sweep. When a candidate is asked why so few genuinely old Cabernet vines exist in Napa, this is the answer.
